clue.text: Foreign minister's transition periods

indicators.note: what is foreign is strange and unfamiliar, so the following word's letters appear in an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: taken as written, all eight letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A government minister from abroad is serving in temporary posts.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Interims are temporary intervals or stopgap arrangements between one settled state and the next.

clue.text: Playing nice new record, 'Firestarter'

indicators.note: playing about with something moves its parts, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a diary is a daily record

explanation.surface: A band plays its nice new record, the song 'Firestarter'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firestarter' is the Prodigy's 1996 hit, but here it simply means an arsonist.
explanation.definitionFit: An incendiary is a person or device that deliberately sets fires, an arsonist or fire-bomb.

clue.text: Least cool women's smallest clothes

indicators.note: to clothe something is to wrap it up, so the longer word wraps the letter

blocks.note: titchy is British slang for tiny

explanation.surface: The least fashionable item in the women's range is the tiniest clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' reads as a noun, but it is the verb meaning to dress or wrap.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone twitchy is nervous and jumpy, the opposite of being calm and composed.

clue.text: Red has drink during revolutionary song

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the song is read backwards
a drink taken during the song falls in its middle

explanation.surface: A communist has a drink while singing a revolutionary anthem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' suggests a communist, which suits the revolutionary song, but it is a wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioja is a Spanish wine, mostly red, from the region of that name.

clue.text: Weirdly calm mediator, with emotions running high

indicators.note: acting weirdly means behaving oddly, so the letters fall into an odd order

explanation.surface: A peacemaker, oddly, is calm while tempers are rising.
explanation.definitionFit: Melodramatic behaviour is exaggerated and overemotional, like a stage melodrama.

clue.text: Off-peak drop in crew members vehicle oddly ignored

indicators.note: the letters in odd positions are passed over, leaving only the even-numbered ones

blocks.note: ABs are able seamen, members of a ship's crew

explanation.surface: Crew members drop down during quiet hours, leaving their vehicle unattended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off-peak' is not about quiet times: it means coming down off a mountain peak.
explanation.definitionFit: Abseiling is descending a rock face by rope, a controlled drop down from a summit.

clue.text: Want to break boxer's nose with hit, which shows a good fighter

indicators.note: the nose is the front of the face, so only the opening letter is wanted
breaking into something means getting inside it

blocks.note: to belt is to hit hard

explanation.surface: Someone longs to break a boxer's nose with a punch, proving they can fight.
explanation.definitionFit: In judo and karate the black belt is the rank awarded to an expert, so wearing one marks skill.

clue.text: Make tea or coffee in this, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling that matches it is wanted

blocks.note: an urn is a big vessel for hot drinks

explanation.surface: An instruction to brew tea or coffee in this pot, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make tea' looks like one phrase; 'Make' alone is the definition, as in making money.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a sum is to gain it as income, as in making a good salary.

clue.text: Dirty residence half scrubbed up

indicators.note: with half scrubbed off, only half the word's letters remain
in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A filthy house has been half cleaned.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty jokes are crude and sexual, which is what lewd means: obscene or indecent.

clue.text: Spicy pepper in pan in South American country

indicators.note: one item placed in another means it sits within the second word's letters

blocks.note: a pot is a cooking pan

explanation.surface: A spicy pepper is cooking in a pan somewhere in South America.
explanation.definitionFit: A chipotle is a smoke-dried jalapeño, a hot chilli used in Mexican cooking.

clue.text: What street vendor might use in pub altercation

blocks.note: a row is a noisy quarrel

explanation.surface: A street trader gets mixed up in a fight at the local pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A barrow here is a costermonger's handcart, from which British street traders sell fruit and vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: Market traders traditionally sell goods from a wheeled cart pushed through the streets.

clue.text: This area's for walking dog, said policeman brooking no nonsense

indicators.note: said means spoken out loud, so a word sounding the same is wanted

blocks.note: a Peke is a Pekingese dog
a strict person will not tolerate nonsense

explanation.surface: A dog-walking area, according to a no-nonsense police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Peak District is a national park in northern England popular with hikers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Peak District is Britain's first national park, much visited for hiking and hill-walking.

clue.text: Tied down repeatedly

blocks.note: to neck a drink is to down it quickly
the same word again, joined by a conjunction

explanation.surface: Something was tied down over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tied down' looks like one phrase, but 'Tied' alone is the definition; 'down' is the slangy verb for drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Racers level with each other are said to be this idiom, meaning exactly even, as in a horse race.

clue.text: Exquisite items from factory with zero emission of gas

blocks.note: the letter that looks like zero
a crude word for breaking wind

explanation.surface: Fine goods come from a factory with no gas emissions.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a clean, green plant, but the gas is bodily.
explanation.definitionFit: Paintings, sculptures and other fine creations are pieces made with great skill and beauty.

clue.text: Distinguished company sing about earl, boring King Edward

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards
boring means drilling into, so these letters go inside the royal pair

blocks.note: taken as written, then read backwards
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A distinguished choir sings about an earl, which bores King Edward.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward suggests a monarch or the British potato variety, but the words split into separate abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A recognised expert is acknowledged and honoured, so distinguished in the sense of eminent.

clue.text: Cake-maker, say, drinking one more bitter

indicators.note: one who is drinking takes something inside, so a letter goes into the middle

blocks.note: someone who ices a cake, 'say' showing this is one kind of cake-maker

explanation.surface: A baker who has been drinking turns more sour.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter weather is very cold, so a more bitter wind is chillier, frostier.

clue.text: Like filling tripe and grouse cut on a Sunday?

indicators.note: a filling goes inside, so this short word is placed within the next

blocks.note: tripe and rot both mean nonsense
a beef is a complaint, as is a grouse

explanation.surface: Tripe and grouse are offered as the Sunday meat dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Tripe and grouse both look like foods, but here they mean nonsense and a gripe. Roast beef is the classic British Sunday lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Roast beef is the traditional joint of meat served for the British Sunday lunch, so a meat cut.

clue.text: Bit of a joint bloke's rolling inhaled by queen

indicators.note: something rolling tumbles over and over, so these letters are jumbled
what is inhaled goes inside, so the jumbled letters sit within the royal name

explanation.surface: A man is rolling a joint and the queen is inhaling it.
explanation.walkthrough: The drug-smoking picture misleads: the joint is a body joint. A bloke is a man in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The talus, or ankle bone, forms part of the ankle joint linking leg and foot.

clue.text: Revered African, saving time, runs a trip in Africa?

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it inside, so the trip's letters hold another letter

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a safari is an expedition, typically in Africa; the question mark marks the example

explanation.surface: An admired African, saving time, hurries off on an expedition across the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: Ras Tafari was the name of Haile Selassie before he was crowned Emperor of Ethiopia; Rastafarians revere him.
explanation.definitionFit: Haile Selassie, known before his coronation by this title and name, is worshipped as divine by Rastafarians.

clue.text: Cycling around Asian city, or the local capital

indicators.note: going round in a cycle moves letters from the front of the word to its back

blocks.note: Kyoto, the old imperial city of Japan

explanation.surface: Someone cycling round an Asian city, or perhaps the local capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asian city' looks like the definition, but it is the city to be cycled; 'local' means the capital of the same country, Japan. Move its last two letters to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Tokyo is the capital of Japan, so for anyone in Kyoto it is the national capital nearby.

clue.text: The urban area here contains light Scottish flora

indicators.note: a phrase that contains something holds it inside its own letters

blocks.note: the town here is this town
an LED, a light-emitting diode, is a light

explanation.surface: A town is home to delicate Scottish plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light Scottish flora' wants to be the definition, but 'light' is wordplay. The thistle is Scotland's national emblem.
explanation.definitionFit: Thistledown is the fluffy seed-head material of the thistle, the plant famously linked with Scotland.

clue.text: What could put you under intensive therapy, in part

indicators.note: only a part of the phrase is used, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Something in intensive care that could knock you out.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was an early general anaesthetic, used to render a patient unconscious before surgery.

clue.text: Business's ending belly up, getting black mark

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter
in a down entry, up means reading from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A firm goes bust in the end and gets a blot on its record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belly up' suggests a business failing, but the phrase splits into a body part and a direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut is a particle of soot or dirt that leaves a dark smudge.

clue.text: Way to disregard liberal viewer's complaint

indicators.note: disregarding a letter means leaving it out of the word

blocks.note: a style is a manner or way

explanation.surface: A way to ignore a liberal television viewer's grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewer' suggests a TV watcher, but it is an eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, an ailment of the organ that sees.

clue.text: Cambridge University figure's winter warmer

blocks.note: the Massachusetts Institute of Technology is in Cambridge, Massachusetts

explanation.surface: A Cambridge academic figure is wrapped up for winter.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambridge suggests the English university, but this is the American Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitten is a glove without separate fingers, worn to keep the hands warm in cold weather.

clue.text: Drunken idiot receiving Murray's first service

indicators.note: the fool receiving something takes it in among its letters
first asks for the opening letter of the tennis player's name only

explanation.surface: A drunk fool takes Andy Murray's first serve at tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: Andy Murray is a British tennis champion, so 'service' first suggests a serve, but it is a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: High Mass is the most elaborate form of the Catholic Eucharist, a church service with music and incense.

clue.text: Peer around Eastbourne, not content to drive

indicators.note: one word placed around others encloses them
without its content the town keeps only its outer shell of letters

blocks.note: a toff is an upper-class person, such as a peer

explanation.surface: An aristocrat goes round the seaside town of Eastbourne, not happy with the drive.
explanation.walkthrough: Eastbourne is an English south-coast resort; a toff is British slang for a posh person. 'Drive' is the golf shot.
explanation.definitionFit: To tee off is to strike the opening shot from the tee in golf, typically a drive.

clue.text: Papers about case of turpitude judge went over again

indicators.note: papers about something wrap round it, holding it inside
a case is the outer covering, so only the outside letters of the word count

blocks.note: to rate is to assess or judge

explanation.surface: Newspapers covering a depravity case say the judge went over it again.
explanation.definitionFit: To iterate is to repeat, perform or say again, so something iterated has been gone over a second time.
